blocks.term: 10Y UST — the benchmark that prices everything
bullets: US govt 10-year borrowing cost — today 5.24%, fell 5bps
Called the 'benchmark' because almost every other asset is priced relative to it: mortgages, corporate bonds, equity discount rates
Mechanically: when investors BUY Treasuries → price rises → yield falls; when they SELL → price falls → yield rises
5.24% today is historically elevated — pre-2022 decade it sat 1-3% for over a decade
Today's 5bp fall despite ongoing geopolitical risk = market pricing in oil supply relief → inflation coming down → fewer Warsh hikes needed
Every 100bps move in 10Y ≈ 8-10% compression or expansion in S&P 500 valuation (all else equal)
The 10Y also anchors mortgage rates — 10Y at 5.24% typically means 30Y fixed mortgage ~7.0-7.5%
blocks.so_what: Your day on a rates desk starts here — the 10Y open sets the tone for every trade, every client call, every product pricing decision that day.

bullets: 2Y fell 10bps today to 4.78% — double the move in the 10Y
2Y yield moves almost in lockstep with Fed funds rate expectations over the next 2 years
2s10s spread = 10Y minus 2Y = today: 5.24% - 4.78% = +46bps (positive = normal slope)
When 2Y falls faster than 10Y, curve is 'bull flattening' — market pricing sooner Fed cuts
The 2022-2024 inversion (2Y > 10Y, spread hit -107bps) correctly predicted economic slowdown
Today's 2Y move > 10Y move = soft-landing narrative strengthening: SPR + Saudi action → oil lower → inflation lower → Fed cuts come forward
Key insight: the 2Y doesn't need the Fed to actually cut — just for markets to PRICE cuts — then 2Y falls
blocks.so_what: If you're watching one number to read the market's Fed view, it's the 2Y yield — it's a real-time probability-weighted bet on where the Fed will be.

blocks.term: Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) — government's oil lever
bullets: US emergency crude stockpile stored in salt caverns in Texas and Louisiana — ~360M barrels currently (~3.5 days of global demand)
G7 countries coordinating releases = pooling capacity from US, EU, Japan, UK, Canada, Australia
Every 1M barrel/day of extra supply roughly pushes WTI down $5-8 over 30 days
Limitation: SPR is a finite stock, not a flow — it buys time but doesn't fix the underlying supply problem (Strait of Hormuz closure)
Market reaction today: oil dropped ~2-3% on announcement → 10Y and 2Y yields fell in sympathy (less inflation risk)
The 2022 SPR release (Biden) was 180M barrels over 6 months — largest in history — only temporarily capped $120 Brent
Warsh is watching: if SPR release sustainably pushes oil below $90, core PCE path improves, he has cover to pause hikes
blocks.so_what: SPR news is a direct input to your inflation forecast — and your inflation forecast is a direct input to your rate positioning. Track oil after every SPR announcement to see if the supply impulse is actually holding.

blocks.term: Strait of Hormuz + Red Sea — why geography moves markets
bullets: Strait of Hormuz: 21-mile wide channel between Iran and Oman — 20% of global oil and 17% of LNG must pass through it
Red Sea / Bab el-Mandeb: route connecting Europe/Americas to Asia via Suez Canal — ~12% of global trade volume
Houthi attacks (2024-2026): forced ships to reroute around Africa's Cape of Good Hope, adding 12 extra days and $1M+ per voyage
Iran partial Hormuz closure (2026): primary driver of WTI jumping from $72 (early 2025) to $100+
Supply shock math: closing even 15% of Hormuz flow = removing 3M+ barrels/day from 100M/day market = instant 5-10% price spike
Saudi assault today targeting Houthi positions to restore Red Sea navigation — if successful, shipping normalizes → WTI falls toward $85
Geopolitical risk premium: markets currently pricing ~$15-20/barrel 'conflict insurance' above fundamental oil value
blocks.so_what: Every S&T morning call starts with Middle East headlines because oil → CPI → Fed path → every asset price. Strait of Hormuz is the single geographic point that can change the Fed's calculus overnight.

bullets: VIX = CBOE's measure of implied 30-day S&P 500 volatility derived from options prices
16.39 today is in the 'calm' zone — barely moved (+0.05) despite active geopolitical headlines
Level calibration: <15 = complacent; 15-20 = mild concern; 20-30 = elevated; 30+ = fear; 40+ = crisis (COVID peaked 85, 2022 hiked to 38)
VIX flat at 16 while Saudi military action unfolds = market saying: 'this is known risk, already priced, not systemic'
VIX + equities up + yields down = classic 'goldilocks' signal — markets treating today as soft-landing progress
Low VIX = options are cheap = smart time to buy protection (puts, collars) before a catalyst changes sentiment
On S&T desks: VIX informs vol surface pricing, options structuring, and hedge fund client conversations about tail risk
blocks.so_what: VIX at 16 with geopolitical news is a confidence signal — the market isn't scared. But that complacency can flip: if Saudi action escalates unexpectedly, VIX can spike from 16 to 28 in a day, crushing vol sellers.

blocks.term: Bull flattening — today's yield curve move decoded
bullets: 'Bull' = bond prices rising (yields falling) — opposite of 'bear' where yields rise
'Flattening' = 2s10s spread narrowing (short and long rates converging toward each other)
Today: 2Y -10bps, 10Y -5bps → 2Y fell MORE → spread narrowed → bull flattening
Signal: market pulling forward rate cut expectations (2Y is most sensitive to near-term Fed expectations)
Contrast with 2026's dominant pattern: 'bear steepening' where 10Y rose faster than 2Y = inflation/fiscal fears pushing long end up
One day's bull flattening doesn't flip the macro narrative — need sustained 2Y rally and 10Y stability to confirm
P&L implication: long 2Y Treasuries made money today; long 30Y Treasuries made money but less; short positions in 2Y hurt most
blocks.so_what: Know these four terms cold for interviews: bull flattener, bear flattener, bull steepener, bear steepener. Every yield curve move is one of these four, and each tells a different macro story.

blocks.term: DXY at 102.65 — what dollar weakness means
bullets: DXY = basket of 6 currencies vs. USD; 57.6% EUR, 13.6% JPY, 11.9% GBP, 9.1% CAD, 4.2% SEK, 3.6% CHF
102.65 is a relatively weak dollar — peaked near 115 in Sept 2022 during peak hawkish Fed expectations
USD weakened today (-0.11) alongside falling US yields: lower rate expectations → less reason to hold USD
Why dollar weakens when rates fall: investors hold USD partly for the high yield; cut that yield, money flows to higher-yielding currencies
USD at 102 is positive for: US multinationals (foreign earnings worth more when converted back), EM economies (easier to service USD debt), gold (cheaper in foreign currencies = more demand)
USD at 102 is negative for: US exporters (less competitive), anyone who shorted EM expecting USD strength
Hub uses EUR/USD as DXY proxy — they move opposite: EUR/USD up today = DXY down = USD weakening
blocks.so_what: Dollar weakness is one of the clearest 'risk-on' signals. When DXY falls, check if equities, EM, commodities, and high-yield are also rallying — they usually are, and it confirms the macro narrative.

blocks.term: Disinflation trade — the narrative running today's markets
bullets: Disinflation = inflation still positive but FALLING (e.g., PCE dropping from 3.3% toward 2%)
Different from deflation (negative inflation) which is far more dangerous and destabilizing
Today's chain: Saudi/G7 action → oil lower → gas prices lower → CPI/PCE lower → fewer Warsh hikes → 2Y yields fall → equities bid
The 'soft landing' trade = disinflation without recession — economy slows just enough to kill inflation but not jobs
Warsh's problem: he made the Volcker/Powell 2021 mistake explicitly — he refuses to declare victory prematurely, even if one data point looks good
Market vs. Fed tension: market is pricing soft landing (equities up, VIX low, 2Y falling); Warsh is still hawkish (3.75-4.00%, signals Oct hike)
One coordinated SPR release doesn't change the structural supply problem — if Strait of Hormuz reopens, narrative accelerates; if it doesn't, today's move reverses
blocks.so_what: Every day you're asking: is the market right to price a soft landing, or is Warsh going to keep hiking and break something? Today's price action is a vote for soft landing — the data will adjudicate.

blocks.term: Equity breadth — why 'the market is up 0.74%' is incomplete
bullets: S&P 500 +0.74% today, but headline masks 'selective risk-on' — Linde (industrial chemicals) outperforming
Breadth = what percentage of stocks are participating in a rally
Narrow rally (few mega-caps dragging index) = fragile, likely to reverse; wide rally = healthy momentum
Linde outperforming = industrial/infrastructure play, not pure risk appetite — defensive tilt within a 'risk-on' day
Market concentration risk: top 10 S&P stocks ≈ 35% of index — NVDA/MSFT/AAPL can move the index even if 490 stocks are flat
Breadth indicators: advance-decline line (how many stocks up vs. down), % of stocks above 50-day MA, equal-weight vs cap-weight SPY divergence
If S&P is up but equal-weighted S&P is flat or down: index rally is driven by a few large caps, not broad recovery
blocks.so_what: On an equities sales desk, you never say 'the market is up.' You say 'the market is up but breadth is narrow with defensive leadership' — that's the actual signal, and it's what your buy-side clients need to hear.

narrative: The Oct 3 brief was a soft-landing story in real time: G7 SPR release + Saudi military action on Houthis signaled oil supply recovery, triggering a bull flattening in the Treasury curve (2Y -10bps, 10Y -5bps) as markets pulled forward Fed cut expectations. But the signal is conditional — one day's oil relief doesn't fix a structural Hormuz closure, VIX at 16 reflects comfort not conviction, and Warsh has given no indication he'll pause. The market is voting for disinflation; Warsh needs the data to confirm it before he'll follow.
